newsitem.title: CANADA: Buoyant Canada energy industry facing higher costs.
newsitem.headline: Buoyant Canada energy industry facing higher costs.

text.p: The hot operating climate in Canada's energy industry has become a double-edged sword for oil and gas companies as booming activity has driven up the costs of drilling and producing, senior executives and analysts said on Monday.

"Rig rates are 20 to 30 percent higher than what they were a couple of years ago. And all services are up, land prices are up -- the whole bit," Anderson Exploration Ltd Chief Executive J.C. Anderson told reporters at the Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers investment symposium.
"The cost of doing business is higher."

Anderson is one of several executives that told analysts and portfolio managers at the conference on Monday that his firm's finding and development and operating costs were not expected to be below last year's.
Anderson posted finding and development costs in 1996 of C$7.04 per barrel of oil equivalent of proven reserves.
A record drilling pace this year in western Canada has pushed the available number of rigs to capacity and has stretched the availablity of oil service companies.
The Canadian Association of Oilwell Drilling Contractors has predicted the industry will drill 14,300 wells this year, 13 percent above the record 12,695 drilled in 1996.

"More than one producer has brought up that their finding and development costs are going to be up year-over-year, everything else being equal, simply because the cost of the inputs are up, in some cases significantly," Matt Janisch, analyst with Nesbitt Burns, told Reuters.
Janisch said higher costs would not have a major impact on 1997 financial results for the oils as a group if oil and gas prices remained strong for the balance of the year.
